newsitem.title: USA: Dlr gains may allow Fed to postpone hike in rates.
newsitem.headline: Dlr gains may allow Fed to postpone hike in rates.

text.p: The dollar's rapid ascent to levels not seen in a number of years against the mark and yen could act as a substitute for higher interest rates and delay a broadly anticipated rate hike by the Federal Reserve in 1997, economists said.
A rising dollar has a disinflationary impact and slows the economy, as do higher interest rates. But the dollar's influence to date has been minimal, analysts said.

"Other things equal, it would certainly tip the Fed into not raising interest rates," said David Wyss, a research director at DRI/McGraw Hill. "It's always on the radar screen...but right now it's not a big deal."

Most economists expect Fed policymakers to leave rates unchanged at the upcoming February 4 and 5 Federal Open Market Committee meeting. However, a Reuters poll shows that a significant number foresee a rate rise at the March confab.
San Francisco Fed President Robert Parry told reporters on Wednesday that the dollar's strength was helping the Fed control inflation.

"One of the things that works in the direction of maybe taking a little bit of pressure off our resources is a higher value of the dollar," he said. "As a result, it's a factor that maybe keeps a little bit of downward pressure on inflation as well."

History shows a significant rise in the dollar, after a prolonged lag, is disinflationary because it reduces import prices and the total value of export sales. Also, economic growth slows as exports are curtailed.
Raising lending rates would steepen this slowdown and price drop by pushing the dollar higher, analysts said.

"The Fed clearly wouldn't want to encourage further dollar gains by raising the interest rate. It could slow down the economy too much," said Don Ratajczak, director of economic forecasting center at Georgia State University.
The dollar has appreciated almost 50 percent since its post-World War II low of 79.75 yen, and roughly 22 percent from its nadir of 1.3438 marks, both seen in March-April of 1995.
So far, this prolonged dollar rise has only dampened import prices and hurt the trade balance in specific industry sectors, like automobiles, economists said.

"I don't think the dollar's level is turning out to be much of a hindrance to us at this point," said William Griggs, managing director at Griggs & Santow Inc and a former financial economist at the Dallas Fed.

The United States' relatively small amount of imports compared to Gross Domestic Product and the fact that the price of most major commodity imports, such as oil, are denominated in dollars insulates the United States from foreign exchange risk, analysts said.
Imports account for roughly 11 to 12 percent of U.S. GDP, significantly lower than the 30 percent average for European countries, said Ian Shepardson, chief economist at HSBC Markets Inc.
Also, current U.S. inflation worries are centered more on wages, which are independent of exchange rates, than prices.
"The primary inflation worry is really what is happening to wages, not prices," Wyss said.

Highlighting the impact currency strength can have on monetary policy, British Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said last week that the strength of sterling was a key factor in his decision to leave rates unchanged.
Experts believe Fed policymakers may come to a similar conclusion about U.S. rates later this year.
